title: The thunderous silence
hookLine: asked about non-duality, the bodhisattvas answer in words; Vimalakirti stays silent

lines: A QUESTION GOES AROUND THE ROOM.
cards: A question goes around a room, and everyone gets a turn. One by one, the guests in Vimalakirti's sickroom give their answers, each one careful and good.
Then the question comes back to the host, the sick layman lying on his couch. The room waits. And he says nothing at all.
No shrug, no smile, no meaningful look. Just nothing. And the guest who asked him, the bodhisattva of wisdom himself, calls that nothing the real answer.

teach.b: Here's the question. Vimalakirti asks the bodhisattvas gathered around him: how does a bodhisattva enter the teaching of non-duality? The doorway, the sutra calls it.
They answer one at a time. Each names a pair the mind is used to splitting, birth and death, self and other, pure and impure, this world and nirvana, and shows how the pair isn't really two.
It's a lovely, patient stretch of the sutra, answer after answer, each one true.
Non-duality, he says, is where nothing is spoken, explained, pointed to or known. It's beyond every word. Then he turns to the host: we've all given our answers; now you tell us.
And Vimalakirti is silent. Excellent, excellent, says Manjushri. This is the real entry into non-duality, where words and letters have no place.
Here's the difference. Manjushri's answer was right, but he still had to use words to say it. Vimalakirti's silence doesn't describe the doorway.
Some later readers in East Asia call it a silence like thunder.
And it isn't the silence of someone who doesn't know, or someone sulking, or dodging. It comes last, after every other answer has been said in full, in reply to a real question.
The silence lands because of all the words before it. In daily life, it can be the moment after a friend finishes telling something hard, when any answer would make it smaller.

how: Mahayana Buddhists read Vimalakirti's silence as a teaching about the limits of words, and in Chan and Zen communities it is retold as a model of answering without explaining.

o: a wordless answer given after every other answer
a loud drum chant that ends in a sudden hush
the quiet after a teacher refuses to answer

games.q: the thunderous silence: tap the pairs.
p: each shows a pair isn't really two
the name later readers gave it

s: Vimalakirti stays silent because he doesn't know the answer
Manjushri praises the silence as the real entry into non-duality.
Manjushri's own answer was that non-duality is beyond words
right, but he still said it in words. then he turned to Vimalakirti.
the silence comes before anyone else answers
it comes last, after every guest has spoken.

games.q: you're Vimalakirti. every guest has answered, and Manjushri asks for yours. what do you do?
games.why: he is silent, and Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, calls it the real entry into non-duality, where words have no place.

practice: Ask yourself one plain question: what is here, right now? Let the answers rush in, words and labels and little explanations, and set each one down without arguing.
Then ask again and don't answer at all; just stay with the sounds, the weight of the body, the breath going in and out.

wordCard.voice: The thunderous silence. Vimalakirti's wordless answer to the question of non-duality, given after every other answer had been spoken. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: silence, the quiet of a sage. the sutra's own wording for Vimalakirti's silence may differ.

carryVoice: Your line: thunderous silence. Sometimes the fullest answer has no words in it. Until tomorrow.
